A characterization of braided enriched monoidal categories
Zachary Dell

Abstract
. We construct an equivalence between the 2-categories 𝓥 ​ MonCat G 𝒜 \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}} of rigid 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -monoidal categories for a braided monoidal category 𝒱 \mathcal{V} and 𝓥 ​ ModTens G 𝒜 \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}} of oplax braided functors from 𝒱 \mathcal{V} into the Drinfeld centers of ordinary rigid monoidal categories. The 1-cells in each are the respective lax monoidal functors, and the 2-cells are the respective monoidal natural transformations. Our proof also gives an equivalence in the case that we consider only strong monoidal 1-cells on both sides. The 2-categories 𝓥 ​ MonCat G 𝒜 \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}} and 𝓥 ​ ModTens G 𝒜 \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}} have G G -graded analogues. We also get an equivalence of 2-categories between G G -extensions of some fixed 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -monoidal category 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , and G G -extensions of some fixed 𝒱 \mathcal{V} -module tensor category ( A , ℱ A Z ) (A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}) .



1.
Introduction

The theory of monoidal categories enriched in a symmetric monoidal category
\mathcal{V}
is well established
[
Str83
,
Kel05
,
Str05
,
GP18
]
. The articles (
[
MP19
,
MPP18
,
JMPP19
]
) have developed the theory when
\mathcal{V}
need only be braided, without symmetry. Remark 5.2 of
[
JS93
]
outlines the idea of braided enriched categories and mentions that they form a 2-category. Braided enriched monoidal categories were classified in
[
MP19
]
in terms of strongly unital oplax braided monoidal functors from the enriching category
\mathcal{V}
into the Drinfeld center of an ordinary monoidal category:

Theorem 1.1

(
[
MP19
]
)
.

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a braided monoidal category.
There is a bijective correspondence

\left\{\,\parbox{142.26378pt}{\rm Rigid $\mathcal{V}$-monoidal categories $\mathcal{A}$, such that $x\mapsto\mathcal{A}(1_{\mathscr{C}}\to x)$ admits a left adjoint}\,\left\}\,\,\,\,\cong\,\,\left\{\,\parbox{227.62204pt}{\rm Pairs $\left(A,\mathcal{F}^{\scriptscriptstyle Z}\right)$ with $A$ a rigid monoidal category and $\mathcal{F}_{A}^{\scriptscriptstyle Z}:\mathcal{V}\to Z\left(A\right)$ braided oplax monoidal, such that $\mathcal{F}_{A}\coloneqq\mathcal{F}_{A}^{\scriptscriptstyle Z}\circ R$ admits a right adjoint}\,\right\},\right.\right.

where
R:Z\left(A\right)\to A
is the forgetful functor.

Note that we are writing composition from left to right, as in
[
MP19
,
MPP18
]
, but reversed to the typical convention. From a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category
\mathcal{A}
, we can take the underlying category
A
, which has the same objects as
\mathcal{A}
and hom sets
A\left(a\to b\right)\coloneqq\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\right)
. The underlying category of
\mathcal{A}
is denoted by
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}
in
[
MP19
]
, but here we merely change the font; there are no ambiguous situations, and our focus is not on the distinction between
\mathcal{A}
and its underlying category
A
. As shown in
[
MP19
]
,
\mathcal{F}_{A}
is taken to be the left adjoint of
A\left(1_{A}\to{-}\right)
and shown to lift to
\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}:\mathcal{V}\to Z\left(A\right)
.
In the other direction, given
\left(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}\right)
we can construct a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category
\mathcal{A}
using the same objects as
A
, and hom objects defined via the Yoneda lemma by the natural isomorphisms

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}\left(v\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\right)\cong A\left(a\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)\to b\right),

which themselves follow from rigidity and the right adjoint of
\mathcal{F}
.
The article
[
MPP18
]
characterizes when the functor
\mathcal{F}^{Z}
is in fact
strong
monoidal, and also develops a notion of completeness for
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories. In the absence of monoidal structures,
[
MP19
]
states an equivalence of 2-categories; we go one categorical level higher to the case of
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories:

Theorem 1.2
.

Theorem
1.1
extends to an equivalence of 2-categories.

This theorem was announced in
[
JMPP19
]
. A recent article,
[
KYZZ21
]
, contains similar results with independent proofs. To start, we construct 2-categories with the sets from Theorem
1.1
as 0-cells as follows:

•

The 1-cells on the left hand side are lax
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functors.

•

The 1-cells on the right are lax monoidal functors equipped with an extra
action-coherence
natural transformation, introduced in Section
3
. The action-coherence natural transformation encodes the interaction between the functor
\mathcal{F}^{Z}
, which is
oplax
, and the 1-cells, which are
lax
.

•

On both sides, 2-cells are the corresponding monoidal natural transformations satisfying the appropriate coherences with the action coherence natural transformations.

We then construct a 2-functor between the 2-categories, proceeding as in
[
MP19
]
on 0-cells. The map on 2-cells turns out to be straightforward, so the bulk of our work goes into constructing the map on 1-cells between the two 2-categories, verifying that the maps together form a 2-functor, and showing that this 2-functor is a 2-equivalence. Starting with a lax
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functor
\mathcal{R}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
between
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories, we get an ordinary lax monoidal functor by taking the underlying functor
R=\mathcal{R}^{\mathcal{V}}
, and we construct our action-coherence natural transformation
r:F_{B}\to R\circ F_{A}
via, for
v\in\mathcal{V}
,

, Theorem

]
the authors introduce the notions of a

-monoidal category for a finite group

[

,

,

. In Section

we introduce the necessary definitions and lift Theorem

to the

-graded setting. Then in Section

we go one step further to the case of
G
-extensions of
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories, and again lift Theorem
1.2
.

2.
Background

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a braided monoidal category with braiding
\beta
. We follow the notational conventions set in
[
MP19
]
; specifically, we suppress
\otimes
(in
\mathcal{V}
) and all associators and unitors in
\mathcal{V}
, with compositions written explicitly as
\circ
, and composition written from left to right.

2.1.
\mathcal{V}
-categories

A
\mathcal{V}
-category, or
\mathcal{V}
-enriched category,
\mathcal{A}
consists of a collection of objects along with:

•

For each pair of objects
a,b\in\mathcal{A}
, an associated hom object
\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\in\mathcal{V}
,

•

For each object
a\in\mathcal{A}
, an identity element
j_{a}\in\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to a\right)\right)
, and

•

For each triple of objects
a,b,c\in\mathcal{A}
, a distinguished composition morphism

\displaystyle{-}\circ_{\mathcal{A}}{-}\in\mathcal{V}\left(\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\mathcal{A}\left(b\to c\right)\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to c\right)\right)

satisfying the axioms

•

Unitality: For all
a,b\in\mathcal{A}
,

For objects
a,b
in a
\mathcal{V}
-enriched category
\mathcal{A}
and
v\in\mathcal{V}
, a
v
-graded morphism
from
a
to
b
is a morphism
f\in\mathcal{V}\left(v\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\right)
. We will give particular attention to the case where
v=1_{\mathcal{V}}
, the
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded morphisms
.

Example 2.1

(Self-enrichment)
.

Given a closed monoidal category
\mathcal{V}
, we can construct a
\mathcal{V}
-category
\widehat{\mathcal{V}}
by starting with the objects of
\mathcal{V}
, then taking hom objects
\widehat{\mathcal{V}}\left(u\to v\right)=\left[u,v\right]
, the internal hom in
\mathcal{V}
defined via

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}\left(uw\to v\right)=\mathcal{V}\left(w\to\widehat{\mathcal{V}}\left(u\to v\right)\right).

j_{v}\coloneqq\mate\left(\id_{v}\right)

Definition 2.2
.

Given a
\mathcal{V}
-category
\mathcal{A}
, we can construct an ordinary category
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}
, the
underlying category
of
\mathcal{A}
, by giving
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}
the same objects as
\mathcal{A}
, defining
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(a\to b\right)\coloneqq\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\right)
for each
a,b\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}
, and composition via
f\circ g=\left(fg\right)\circ\left({-}\circ_{\mathcal{A}}{-}\right)
, for
f\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(a\to b\right)
and
g\in\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(b\to c\right)
. In the following we will often denote the underlying category of a
\mathcal{V}
-category
\mathcal{A}
by a standard font
A
.

2.2.
\mathcal{V}
-functors and natural transformations

A
\mathcal{V}
-functor

\mathcal{R}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
between
\mathcal{V}
-categories consists of a function on objects and for each
a,b\in\mathcal{A}
, a morphism
\mathcal{R}_{a\to b}\in\mathcal{V}\left(\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\to\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\to\mathcal{R}\left(b\right)\right)\right)
, satisfying the following axioms:

We can compose two
\mathcal{V}
-functors
\mathcal{A}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{B}\xrightarrow{\mathscr{S}}\mathscr{C}
via
\left(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathscr{S}\right)\left(a\right)=\mathscr{S}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\right)
and
\left(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathscr{S}\right)_{a\to b}=\mathcal{R}_{a\to b}\circ\mathscr{S}_{\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\to\mathcal{R}\left(b\right)}
for all objects
a,b\in\mathcal{A}
.
For
\mathcal{V}
-functors
\mathcal{R},\mathscr{S}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
, we define a
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded natural transformation

\theta:\mathcal{R}\Rightarrow\mathscr{S}
by assigning to each object
a\in\mathcal{A}
a
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded morphism
\theta_{a}\in\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\to\mathscr{S}\left(a\right)\right)\right)
such that that for all
a,b\in\mathcal{A}

This condition is the usual naturality square, but written in terms of composition of
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded morphisms.

Definition 2.3
.

Given a
\mathcal{V}
-functor
\mathcal{R}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
between
\mathcal{V}
-categories, we construct the
underlying functor
of
\mathcal{R}
, an ordinary functor
\mathcal{R}^{\mathcal{V}}:A\to B
between the underlying categories. We take
\mathcal{R}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(a\right)=\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)
for each
a\in A
, and on morphisms
f\in A\left(a\to b\right)=\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\right)
, we define
\mathcal{R}\left(f\right)\coloneqq f\circ\mathcal{R}_{a\to b}\in B\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\to\mathcal{R}\left(b\right)\right)=\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\to\mathcal{R}\left(b\right)\right)\right)
. As with the underlying category, we will often denote
\mathcal{R}^{\mathcal{V}}
by simply
R
.

2.3.
\mathcal{V}
-Monoidal Categories

Given a
\mathcal{V}
-category, we can add a monoidal structure to get a (strict)
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category. We need the additional data of

•

A unit object
1_{\mathcal{A}}
,

•

For each pair
a,b\in\mathcal{A}
, a tensor product object
ab\in\mathcal{A}
, and

•

For each
a,b,c,d\in\mathcal{A}
, a tensor product morphism
{-}\otimes_{\mathcal{A}}{-}\in\mathcal{V}\left(\mathcal{A}\left(a\to c\right)\mathcal{A}\left(b\to d\right)\to\mathcal{A}\left(ab\to cd\right)\right)

such that the following axioms hold:

•

Tensor unit: For all
a\in\mathcal{A}
,
1_{\mathcal{A}}a=a=a1_{\mathcal{A}}
,

•

Associative on objects: For all
a,b,c\in\mathcal{A}
,
\left(ab\right)c=a\left(bc\right)
,

•

Unitality: For all
a,b\in\mathcal{A}
,

Definition 2.4
.

Given a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category
\mathcal{A}
, take the underlying category
A=\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}
. Then
A
inherits the monoidal structure of
\mathcal{A}
via the same tensor product on objects, and for
f\in A\left(a\to c\right)
and
g\in A\left(b\to d\right)
,
fg\coloneqq\left(fg\right)\circ\left({-}\otimes{-}\right)
, where on the right hand side
f
and
g
are viewed as morphisms in
\mathcal{V}
. This is the
underlying monoidal category
of
\mathcal{A}
.

2.4.
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functors and natural transformations

We can similarly extend
\mathcal{V}
-functors to a monoidal setting: a strictly unital
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functor
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right):\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
consists of an underlying
\mathcal{V}
-functor
\mathcal{R}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
with
\mathcal{R}\left(1_{\mathcal{A}}\right)=1_{\mathcal{B}}
and
j_{1_{\mathcal{A}}}^{\mathcal{A}}\circ\mathcal{R}_{1_{\mathcal{A}}\to 1_{\mathcal{A}}}=j_{1_{\mathcal{B}}}^{\mathcal{B}}
, and a family of
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded isomorphisms
\rho_{a,b}^{R}\in\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\mathcal{R}\left(b\right)\to\mathcal{R}\left(ab\right)\right)\right)
satisfying:

We call
\mathcal{R}

lax
if the
\rho_{a,b}^{R}
are not necessarily isomorphisms, and
oplax
if we have
\overline{\rho}_{a,b}^{R}:1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(ab\right)\to\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\mathcal{R}\left(b\right)\right)
instead, again not necessarily isomorphisms, along with the corresponding axioms in place of the above.

We can compose
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right):\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
with
\left(\mathscr{S},\sigma^{S}\right):\mathcal{B}\to\mathscr{C}
to get a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functor via the usual composition on
\mathcal{V}
-functors and laxitor

Definition 2.6
.

Given a (lax)
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functor
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{\mathcal{R}}\right)
between
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
, there is a canonical ordinary (lax) monoidal functor
\left(R,\rho\right)
between the underlying categories
A
and
B
. We take
R
to be the underlying functor, and we take
\rho\coloneqq\rho^{\mathcal{R}}
; notice that for
a,b\in\mathcal{A}
,

\displaystyle\rho_{a,b}^{\mathcal{R}}\in\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\mathcal{R}\left(b\right)\to\mathcal{R}\left(ab\right)\right)\right)=B\left(R\left(a\right)R\left(b\right)\to R\left(ab\right)\right).

We call
\left(R,\rho\right)
the
underlying monoidal functor
of
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{\mathcal{R}}\right)
; verifying the axioms of a (lax) monoidal functor is a useful exercise.

In order for the name “trace” to make sense, we would expect an isomorphism
\Tr_{\mathcal{A}}\left(ab\right)\to\Tr_{\mathcal{A}}\left(ba\right)
. When
\mathcal{A}
is rigid, we have

\displaystyle\Tr_{\mathcal{A}}\left(ab\right)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}\left(1_{\mathcal{A}}\to ab\right)

\displaystyle\cong\mathcal{A}\left(b^{*}\to a\right)

\displaystyle\cong\mathcal{A}\left(1_{\mathcal{A}}\to b^{**}a\right),

so we get a natural isomorphism
\Tr_{\mathcal{A}}\left(ab\right)\cong\Tr_{\mathcal{A}}\left(b^{**}a\right)
. In the case that there is a
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded natural isomorphism
1_{\mathcal{A}}\cong**
(
\mathcal{A}
is
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded pivotal), this is then also isomorphic to
\mathcal{A}\left(1_{\mathcal{A}}\to ba\right)=\Tr_{\mathcal{A}}\left(ba\right)
. With this in mind, we continue the convention in
[
MP19
]
and
[
HPT16
]
to call the map a trace.

2.6.
2-categories, 2-functors, and 2-equivalences

Definition 2.7
.

A
2-category

\mathscr{A}
is a category enriched in
Cat
. Explicitly,
\mathscr{A}
consists of the data

•

A collection of objects. In the 2-categorical context, we will refer to objects as
0-cells
to avoid ambiguity.

•

For each
A,B\in\mathscr{A}
, a
hom-category

\mathscr{A}\left(A\to B\right)
. We avoid the term “morphism” here to avoid confusion, and refer to objects of such a hom-category simply as 1-cells. The morphisms of a hom-category are called
2-cells
. We write
R:A\to B
for 1-cells, and
\theta:R\Rightarrow S
for 2-cells. Vertical composition of 2-cells is suppressed in our notation.

•

For each
A\in\mathscr{A}
, a
unit 1-cell

\id_{A}\in\mathscr{A}\left(A\to A\right)
.

•

For each
A,B,C\in\mathscr{A}
, a composition bifunctor
\circ:\mathscr{A}\left(A\to B\right)\times\mathscr{A}\left(B\to C\right)
. On 1-cells
\circ
is the expected composition, and it is horizontal composition on 2-cells.

satisfying the following axioms:

•

Unitality: For all
A,B\in\mathscr{A}
and each
f\in\mathscr{A}\left(A\to B\right)
,
\id_{A}\circ f=f\circ\id_{B}=f
.

•

Associativity: For each
A,B,C,D\in\mathscr{A}
,

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}\left(A\to B\right)\times\mathscr{A}\left(B\to C\right)\times\mathscr{A}\left(C\to D\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}\left(A\to B\right)\times\mathscr{A}\left(B\to D\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}\left(A\to C\right)\times\mathscr{A}\left(C\to D\right)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}\left(A\to D\right)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\circ\times\id}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id\times\circ}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\circ}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\circ}

commutes.

Definition 2.8
.

A
2-functor

P:\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{B}
between 2-categories
\mathscr{A}
and
\mathscr{B}
is a
Cat
-functor between
Cat
-categories. Explicitly,
P
consists of:

•

For each 0-cell
A\in\mathscr{A}
, a 0-cell
P\left(A\right)
in
\mathscr{B}
.

•

For each pair of 0-cells
A,B
in
\mathscr{A}
, a functor

\displaystyle P_{A\to B}:\mathscr{A}\left(A\to B\right)\to\mathscr{B}\left(P\left(A\right)\to P\left(B\right)\right)

such that

•

For each 0-cell
\mathcal{A}
in
\mathscr{A}
,
P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}}\left(\id_{\mathcal{A}}\right)=\id_{P\left(\mathcal{A}\right)}
.

•

the composition functor is preserved, i.e., given 0-cells
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}
in
\mathscr{A}
:

–

For 1-cells
\mathcal{R}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{S}:\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
,

\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}\left(\mathcal{R}\right)\circ P_{\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}\left(\mathcal{S}\right)=P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{C}}\left(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{S}\right).

–

For 1-cells
\mathcal{R}_{1},\mathcal{R}_{2}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
and
\mathcal{S}_{1},\mathcal{S}_{2}:B\to\mathcal{C}
, and 2-cells
\theta:\mathcal{R}_{1}\Rightarrow\mathcal{R}_{2}
and
\psi:\mathcal{S}_{1}\Rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{2}
,

\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{C}}\left(\theta\psi\right)=P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}\left(\theta\right)P_{\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}\left(\psi\right).

Definition 2.9

(
[
JY20
]
)
.

We say that a 2-functor
P:\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{B}
is a
2-equivalence
if it is:

•

Essentially surjective: For every 0-cell
B\in\mathscr{B}
, there is a 0-cell
A\in\mathscr{A}
and an equivalence of categories
A\simeq P\left(A\right)
.

•

Fully faithful: For each pair of 0-cells
A,B\in\mathscr{A}
,
P_{A\to B}
is an equivalence of categories

3.
The 2-categories
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}

In this section we will construct the 2-categories
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
, based on the 0-cells studied in
[
MP19
]
. First, however, we record some terminology from
[
MPP18
,
JMPP19
]
.

Definition 3.1

(
[
MP19
,
MPP18
,
JMPP19
]
)
.

We call a
\mathcal{V}
-category
\mathcal{A}

•

weakly tensored
if for each
a\in\mathcal{A}
, the representable functor
\mathcal{A}\left(a\to{-}\right):A\to\mathcal{V}
admits a left adjoint.

•

tensored
if for each
a\in\mathcal{A}
, the
\mathcal{V}
-representable functor
\mathcal{A}\left(a\to{-}\right):\mathcal{A}\to\widehat{\mathcal{V}}
admits a left
\mathcal{V}
-adjoint.

Note that we must be able to form the self-enrichment
\widehat{\mathcal{V}}
for the definition of a tensored
\mathcal{V}
-category to make sense; this requires
\mathcal{V}
to be
closed
(see
[
MPP18
]
). In this article we assume
\mathcal{V}
is rigid, and being rigid is a stronger property of a
\mathcal{V}
-category than being closed.

Definition 3.2

(
[
JMPP19
]
defn 2.6, HPT)
.

A
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor category
is a pair
(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})
where
A
is a monoidal category and
\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}:\mathcal{V}\to Z\left(A\right)
is an oplax, strongly unital braided monoidal functor. We call the
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor category
oplax
or
strongly unital
if
\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}
is oplax or strongly unital, respectively.

We say that a
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor category
(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})
is

•

rigid
if
A
is rigid,

•

weakly tensored
if
\mathcal{F}\coloneqq\mathcal{F}^{Z}\circ\Forget_{Z}
admits a right adjoint, with
\Forget_{Z}:Z\left(A\right)\to A
the forgetful functor,

•

tensored
if it is weakly tensored and
\mathcal{F}
is strong monoidal.

Definition 3.3
.

The following data defines a 2-category, which we call
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
:

•

0-Cells are rigid
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories (
\mathcal{A}
,
\mathcal{B}
, etc.) such that the functor
x\mapsto\mathcal{A}\left(1_{\mathcal{A}}\to x\right)
admits a left adjoint.

•

For each pair of 0-cells
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}
, the hom-category
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}\left(\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\right)
consists of

–

1-cells: Strictly unital lax
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functors
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right):\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
, where
\rho^{R}
is the laxitor for
\mathcal{R}
.

–

2-cells:
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded monoidal natural transformations
\theta:\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right)\to\left(\mathcal{S},\sigma^{S}\right)
.

–

Composition is the usual vertical composition of
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded natural transformations:

Composition functors:

–

Two 1-cells
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right):\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
and
\left(\mathcal{S},\sigma^{S}\right):\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
have composition defined via
\left(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{S}\right)\left(a\right)\coloneqq\mathcal{S}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\right)
,
\left(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{S}\right)_{a\to b}\coloneqq\mathcal{R}_{a\to b}\circ\mathcal{S}_{R\left(a\right)\to\mathcal{R}\left(b\right)}
, and composite laxitor

\mathcal{C}\left(R\left(a\right)\to S\left(a\right)\right)
\sigma_{R\left(a\right),R\left(b\right)}^{S}
\mathcal{S}\left(\rho_{a,b}^{R}\right)
{-}\circ_{\mathcal{C}}{-}

•

Lastly, unit 1-cells are the usual identity
\mathcal{V}
-functor
\id_{\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}
along with the identity natural transformations as the tensorator.

Remark 3.4
.

The definition above of
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
does in fact define a 2-category.

•

First,
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}\left(\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\right)
is a category:

–

Unit 2-cells are the usual identity natural transformations, and thus composition preserves units.

–

Vertical composition of 2-cells is associative by Lemma 2.2 of
[
MP19
]
.

•

Composition functors are unital because unit 1-cells are identity
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functors, with their usual composition.

•

Composition functors are associative: Horizontal composition of 2-cells is associative by Lemma 2.3 of
[
MP19
]
, and composition of 1-cells is just ordinary
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functor composition, which is associative.

Definition 3.5
.

We define a second 2-category, which we call
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
, from the following data:

•

0-Cells are weakly tensored
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor categories
(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})
.

•

For each pair of 0-cells
(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}),(B,\mathcal{F}_{B}^{Z})
, we define the hom-category
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}\left((A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})\to(B,\mathcal{F}_{B}^{Z})\right)
as follows:

–

1-cells are triples
\left(R,\rho,r\right):(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})\to(B,\mathcal{F}_{B}^{Z})
, where
\left(R,\rho\right)
is a strictly unital lax monoidal functor, and
r:\mathcal{F}_{B}\Rightarrow\mathcal{F}_{A}\circ R
is a strictly unital monoidal natural transformation, i.e.,
R\left(1_{A}\right)=1_{B}
and
r_{1_{\mathcal{V}}}=\id_{1_{B}}
; they must also satisfy the half-braiding coherence and action coherence conditions:

where
e_{a,\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)}\in\mathcal{B}\left(a\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)\to\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)a\right)
is the half-braiding on
\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)
(from the Drinfeld center), and similarly for
e_{R\left(a\right),\mathcal{F}_{B}\left(v\right)}
.

–

2-cells
\left(R,\rho,r\right)\Rightarrow\left(S,\sigma,s\right)
are monoidal natural transformations
\Theta:\left(R,\rho\right)\to\left(S,\sigma\right)
such that
r_{v}\circ\Theta_{\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)}=s_{v}
.

–

Composition is the usual vertical composition of natural transformations:
\left(\Theta\varphi\right)_{v}=\Theta_{v}\circ\varphi_{v}
.

–

Unit 2-cells are the identity natural transformations.

•

Composition functors:

–

Given
\left(R,\rho,r\right):A\to B
and
\left(S,\sigma,s\right):B\to C
, we form their composite via functor
R\circ S
, laxitor
\sigma_{R\left(a\right),R\left(b\right)}\circ S\left(\rho_{a,b}\right)
and coherence
r_{v}\circ S\left(s_{v}\right)
.

–

If
A,B,C\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
,
R_{1},R_{2}\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}\left(A\to B\right)
,
S_{1},S_{2}\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}\left(B\to C\right)
, and
\Theta:R_{1}\Rightarrow R_{2}
and
\varphi:S_{1}\Rightarrow S_{2}
are 2-cells, the horizontal composite
\Theta\varphi
is defined via

\displaystyle\left(\Theta\varphi\right)_{a}=\varphi_{R_{1}\left(a\right)}\circ S_{2}\left(\Theta_{a}\right).

•

Unit 1-cells:
For each 0-cell
(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
we define the unit 1-cell to be the triple consisting of the identity functor on
A
, the identity laxitor, and the identity natural transformation on
\mathcal{F}_{A}
.

Remark 3.6
.

With the above definition,
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
is a 2-category:

•

For each pair
\left(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}\right),\left(B,\mathcal{F}_{B}^{Z}\right)
of 0-cells in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
,
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}\left(\left(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}\right)\to\left(B,\mathcal{F}_{B}^{Z}\right)\right)
is a category:

–

Unit 2-cells are units under composition, since they are identity natural transformations with the usual composition of natural transformations.

–

Composition of natural transformations is associative.

•

Composition functors are unital because the unit 1-cells are identity functors with identity laxitors and the identity natural transformation for action-coherence.

•

Composition functors are associative because horizontal composition of natural transformations, composition of monoidal functors, and vertical composition of natural transformations are all associative.

4.
Calculations using mates

Given an adjunction
\mathcal{A}\left(\mathcal{L}\left(x\right)\to b\right)\cong\mathcal{B}\left(x\to\mathcal{R}\left(b\right)\right)
and a morphism
f\in\mathcal{A}\left(\mathcal{L}\left(x\right)\to b\right)
, the
mate
of
f
is the corresponding morphism
\mate\left(f\right)\in\mathcal{B}\left(x\to\mathcal{R}\left(b\right)\right)
.

Remark 4.1
.

A large number of our discussions focus on the following adjunction (Adjunction 4.2 in
[
MP19
]
): Let
\mathcal{A}
be a 0-cell in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
. Then for each
a,b\in\mathcal{A}
and each
v\in\mathcal{V}
, we have the adjunction

(4.1)

A\left(a\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)\to b\right)\cong\mathcal{V}\left(v\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\right)

where
A=\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}
is the underlying category of
\mathcal{A}
. In particular, note that when
v=1_{\mathcal{V}}
the adjunction becomes
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(a\to b\right)\cong\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\right)
. In this case, we actually have equality by definition of
\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}
, and, although slightly redundant, we often use a superscript to keep track of which side of this equality adjunction a morphism lives on. There is no ambiguity even without a notational difference, as a quick check of source and target will clear up any confusion.

Definition 4.2
.

We define the
unit
of this adjunction for
v\in\mathcal{V}
as

\displaystyle\eta_{v}^{\mathcal{F}_{A}}\coloneqq\mate\left(\id_{\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)}\right)

and the
counit
of this adjunction for
a,b\in A
as

\displaystyle\epsilon_{a\to b}^{\mathcal{F}_{A}}\coloneqq\mate\left(\id_{\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)}\right),

both under the corresponding version of Adjunction
4.1
.

Notation 4.3
.

We extend a useful notation from
[
MP19
]
:

\displaystyle\left[a\to b;c\to d;\cdots\right]_{\mathcal{F}}^{\mathcal{A}}\coloneqq\mathcal{F}\left(\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\mathcal{A}\left(c\to d\right)\cdots\right),

where
\mathcal{A}
is a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category, and
\mathcal{F}
is any functor from
\mathcal{V}
. Note that
\mathcal{F}
need not be specifically
\mathcal{F}_{A}
, e.g., we use

\displaystyle\left[a\to b;c\to d;\cdots\right]_{\mathcal{F}_{B}}^{\mathcal{A}}\coloneqq\mathcal{F}_{B}\left(\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\mathcal{A}\left(c\to d\right)\cdots\right).

Remark 4.4
.

Under Adjunction
4.1
, the mate of
{-}\circ_{\mathcal{A}}{-}\in\mathcal{V}\left(\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\mathcal{A}\left(b\to c\right)\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to c\right)\right)

We now record several useful lemmas in computing mates; we start with a consequence of naturality.

Lemma 4.5
.

Let
\mathcal{A}\left(\mathscr{L}\left(x\right)\to b\right)\cong\mathcal{B}\left(x\to\mathscr{R}\left(b\right)\right)
be an adjunction. If
f_{1}\in\mathcal{A}\left(\mathscr{L}\left(x\right)\to b\right)
and
f_{2}\in\mathcal{A}\left(b\to c\right)
, then
\mate\left(f_{1}\circ f_{2}\right)=\mate\left(f_{1}\right)\circ\mathscr{R}\left(f_{2}\right)
. Similarly, if
g_{1}\in\mathcal{B}\left(x\to y\right)
and
g_{2}\in\mathcal{B}\left(y\to\mathscr{R}\left(b\right)\right)
, then
\mate\left(g_{1}\circ g_{2}\right)=\mathscr{L}\left(g_{1}\right)\circ\mate\left(g_{2}\right)
. In diagrams,

or

, the oplaxitor

is again an identity. If
u=1_{\mathcal{V}}
or
b=1_{\mathcal{A}}
, then the half-braiding is an identity.

Proof.

From the composition lemma, the mate of
{-}\otimes_{\mathcal{A}}{-}
, and naturality of

Lemma 4.9
.

f\in\mathcal{V}\left(u\to v\right)
, we can consider
\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(f\right)
as a morphism in
\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{A}\left(\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(u\right)\to\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)\right)\right)=A\left(\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(u\right)\to\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)\right)
. Then using Lemmas
4.7
and
4.5

\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(f\right)

5.
The 2-functor

In this section, we construct a map
P:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
and prove that
P
is a 2-functor. In the following section we show that
P
is in fact a 2-equivalence.

5.1.
Map on 0-cells

Our map on 0-cells is the bijective correspondence from
[
MP19
]
: we set
P\left(\mathcal{A}\right)=\left(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{\mathcal{Z}}\right)
, with
A\coloneqq\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{V}}
the underlying category of
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}
the left adjoint of
x\mapsto\mathcal{A}\left(1_{\mathcal{A}}\to x\right)
lifted to the center via the half-braidings

Remark 5.1
.

To lift
\mathcal{F}_{A}
to
\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}
, it is also necessary to show that the images of morphisms in
\mathcal{V}
are morphisms in
Z\left(A\right)
. This was omitted from
[
MP19
]
, so we include the short proof here.

) again, use another braided interchange after adding an identity, and recognize the result as the mate of the right hand side, so that

5.2.
Map on 1-cells: Definition

Given 0-cells
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
and a 1-cell
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right)\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}\left(\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}\right)
, we construct a 1-cell
\left(R,\rho,r\right)
in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}\left(P\left(\mathcal{A}\right)\to P\left(\mathcal{B}\right)\right)
. Define
R:A\to B
to be the underlying functor of
\mathcal{R}
, and define the laxitor
\rho
via, for
a,b\in A
,
\rho_{a,b}\coloneqq\mate\left(\rho_{a,b}^{R}\right)=\rho_{a,b}^{R}
under the identity adjunction

\displaystyle\mathcal{B}\left(R\left(a\right)R\left(b\right)\to R\left(ab\right)\right)=\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to B\left(R\left(a\right)R\left(b\right)\to R\left(ab\right)\right)\right).

Lastly, we define the natural transformation
r
via

(5.2)

r_{v}=\mate\left(\hbox to61.4pt{\vbox to74.38pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 30.70074pt\lower-4.11433pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

Remark 5.2
.

Following immediately from the corresponding properties in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
, we have:

•

The pair
\left(R,\rho\right)
is a monoidal functor.

•

The functor
R
is strictly unital:
R\left(1_{\mathcal{A}}\right)=1_{\mathcal{B}}
.

•

The laxitor
\rho
is strictly unital:
\rho_{1_{\mathcal{A}},a}=\id_{R\left(a\right)}=\rho_{a,1_{\mathcal{A}}}
.

•

The natural transformation
r
is strictly unital:
r_{1_{\mathcal{V}}}=\id_{1_{\mathcal{B}}}
.

Proposition 5.3
.

The natural transformation
r
is in fact natural, i.e., for each
f\in\mathcal{V}\left(u\to v\right)
, we have

All together this proves:

Proposition 5.6
.

The triple
\left(R,\rho,r\right)
is a 1-cell in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
.

5.3.
Map on 2-cells

Suppose we have a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal natural transformation
\theta:\mathcal{R}\Rightarrow\mathcal{S}
, i.e., a 2-cell in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
. We define a 2-cell
P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}\left(\theta\right):R\Rightarrow S
between the corresponding 1-cells in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
via, for each
a\in\mathcal{A}
,
P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}\left(\theta\right)_{a}\coloneqq\mate\left(\theta_{a}\right)
under the identity adjunction

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\to\mathcal{S}\left(a\right)\right)\right)=\mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\to\mathcal{S}\left(a\right)\right).

We write
\Theta_{a}\coloneqq P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}\left(\theta\right)_{a}
for brevity.

Proposition 5.7
.

As defined above,
\Theta
is a 2-cell in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}

Proof.

Naturality and monoidality of
\Theta
follow easily from the corresponding properties in the enriched setting: taking the appropriate mate of each side of the required conditions gives exactly the corresponding condition in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
. It remains to check that
s_{v}\circ\Theta_{\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)}=\rho_{v}
for all
v\in\mathcal{V}
.

From the hexagon axiom in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
, with
a=1_{\mathcal{A}}
and
b=\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)
, we have

Proposition 5.8
.

With the above definitions,
P:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
is a 2-functor.

We will take the remainder of this section to prove the proposition. We need to show that

•

Each
P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}}
preserves unit 1-cells,

•

Each
P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}
is a functor, i.e., vertical composition of 2-cells is preserved

•

Horizontal composition of 2-cells is preserved, and

•

Composition of 1-cells is preserved.

First, note that both
\id_{P\left(\mathcal{A}\right)}
and
P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}}\left(\id_{\mathcal{A}}\right)
are the identity 1-cell on
P\left(\mathcal{A}\right)
, so unit 1-cells are preserved. Next, since
P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}
on 2-cells is simply taking mates under the identity adjunction, it follows easily from the definitions that horizontal and vertical composition of 2-cells are both preserved. The bulk of the work is involved in showing that composition of 1-cells is preserved, i.e.,

\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}\left((\mathcal{R},\rho^{R})\right)\circ P_{\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}\left((\mathcal{S},\sigma^{S})\right)=P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{C}}\left((\mathcal{R},\rho^{R})\circ(\mathcal{S},\sigma^{S})\right).

The left hand side is given by

\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}\left((\mathcal{R},\rho^{R})\right)\circ P_{\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}\left((\mathcal{S},\sigma^{S})\right)

\displaystyle=(\mathcal{R}^{\mathcal{V}},\rho,r)\circ(\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{V}},\sigma,s),

where
\rho
,
\sigma
,
r
, and
s
are as defined in
5.2
, and the right hand side is

\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{C}}\left((\mathcal{R},\rho^{R})\circ(\mathcal{S},\sigma^{S})\right)=P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{C}}\left(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{S},\sigma^{S}\circ S(\rho^{R})\right)=\left(\left(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{S}\right)^{\mathcal{V}},\mate\left(\sigma^{S}\circ S(\rho^{R})\right),t\right),

where
\sigma^{S}\circ S(\rho^{R})
is as defined in
3.5
and
t\coloneqq\mate\left(\eta_{v}^{\mathcal{F}_{A}}\circ(\mathcal{R}_{1_{\mathcal{A}}\to\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(v\right)}\circ\mathcal{S}_{1_{\mathcal{B}}\to\mathcal{R}\left(\mathcal{F}_{A}\left(f\right)\right)})\right)
. Now,
\left(\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{S}\right)^{\mathcal{V}}=\mathcal{R}^{\mathcal{V}}\circ\mathcal{S}^{\mathcal{V}}
, so these are equal as functors. Further, since
\mate\left(\sigma_{c,d}\right)=\sigma_{c,d}^{S}
, we directly have

6.
Equivalence

Proposition 6.1
.

The 2-functor
P:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
as defined above is essentially surjective on 0-cells.

Proof.

To say that
P
is essentially surjective is just to say that for every 0-cell
(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
, there exists a 0-cell
\mathcal{A}\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
such that
P\left(\mathcal{A}\right)\simeq(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})
. This is exactly the main theorem in
[
MP19
]
.
∎

Definition 6.2
.

Let
(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}),(B,\mathcal{F}_{B}^{Z})\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
be 0-cells, and let
\left(R,\rho,r\right):(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})\to(B,\mathcal{F}_{B}^{Z})
be a 1-cell between them. We construct a 1-cell
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right)
in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
such that
P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}\left(\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right)\right)=\left(R,\rho,r\right)
. Since
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
share the same objects as
A
and
B
, respectively, we can define
\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)=R\left(a\right)
for all
a\in\mathcal{A}
. Next, for
a,b\in\mathcal{A}

\mathcal{R}
into a
\mathcal{V}

Lemma 6.5
.

The
\mathcal{V}
-functor
\mathcal{R}
is strictly unital, and the laxitor
\rho^{R}
is strongly unital, i.e.,
\mathcal{R}\left(1_{\mathcal{A}}\right)=1_{\mathcal{B}}
and
\rho_{1_{\mathcal{A}},a}^{R}=\id_{\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)}=\rho_{a,1_{\mathcal{A}}}^{R}
.

Proof.

First,
R
is strictly unital, so
\mathcal{R}\left(1_{\mathcal{A}}\right)=R\left(1_{\mathcal{A}}\right)=1_{\mathcal{B}}
.

Then
\rho
is strongly unital, so

\displaystyle\rho_{1_{\mathcal{A}},a}^{R}

\displaystyle=\mate\left(\rho_{1_{\mathcal{A}},a}\right)=\mate\left(\id_{R\left(a\right)}\right)=j_{a}^{\mathcal{B}}

and similarly for the other side.
∎

which is exactly the mate of the right hand side.
∎

We have proven:

Proposition 6.8
.

The pair
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right)
defined above is a 1-cell in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
.

We’ve constructed a map from 1-cells of
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
to 1-cells of
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
. To show that
P
is essentially surjective on 1-cells, it now suffices to prove the following proposition.

Proposition 6.9
.

For each pair
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}
of 0-cells in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
, the above map is an essential inverse to
P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}
on 1-cells.

Proof.

Starting with a 1-cell
\left(R,\rho,r\right)
in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}\left((A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})\to(B,\mathcal{F}_{B}^{Z})\right)
, we have

\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}}\left(\left(R,\rho,r\right)\right)\coloneqq\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right),

where for
a,b\in A
,
\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)=R\left(a\right)
,
\rho_{a,b}^{R}=\mate\left(\rho_{a,b}\right)=\rho_{a,b}
and
\mathcal{R}_{a\to b}
is defined in
6.1
. Then
(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R})
maps back to
(\boldsymbol{R},\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{r})
, another 1-cell in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
. Now we show that
(\boldsymbol{R},\boldsymbol{\rho},\boldsymbol{r})
and
(R,\rho,r)
are equal as 1-cells.

•

As functors. For
a\in A
,
\boldsymbol{R}\left(a\right)=\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)=R\left(a\right)
. For
a,b\in A
and a morphism
f\in A\left(a\to b\right)=\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{A}\left(a\to b\right)\right)
, we take the same mate of
f\circ\mathcal{R}_{a\to b}
in two different ways. Under adjunction
4.1
, using the definition of
\boldsymbol{R}
as the underlying functor of
\mathcal{R}
, we have

\displaystyle\mate\left(f\circ\mathcal{R}_{a\to b}\right)=\boldsymbol{R}\left(f\right).

Next, we take the same mate via Lemma
4.5
, making use of naturality and unitality of
r
and

Definition 6.10
.

Given a monoidal natural transformation
\Theta:\left(R,\rho,r\right)\Rightarrow\left(S,\sigma,s\right)
, where
\left(R,\rho,r\right)
and
\left(S,\sigma,s\right)
are 1-cells in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}\left(\left(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}\right)\to\left(B,\mathcal{F}_{B}\right)\right)
, we define a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal natural transformation
\theta:\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right)\Rightarrow\left(\mathcal{S},\sigma^{S}\right)
via
\theta_{a}\coloneqq\mate\left(\Theta_{a}\right)=\Theta_{a}
under the identity adjunction

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathcal{B}\left(R\left(a\right)\to S\left(a\right)\right)\right)=B\left(R\left(a\right)\to S\left(a\right)\right).

is a

which is exactly the mate of the right hand side under lemma
4.7
.
∎

Thus we have proven

Proposition 6.12
.

The 2-functor
P
is fully faithful on 2-cells.

In turn, this finishes the proof of our main theorem:

Theorem 6.13
.

The 2-functor
P:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
is a 2-equivalence.

Remark 6.14
.

If we instead demand that all of our lax functors are in fact strong, i.e., we restrict to the subcategories where 1-cells are only the strong monoidal and strong
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functors, then we get a 2-equivalence by the same proof. Showing that a lax monoidal functor is in fact strong is simply a check that the laxitors are invertible, and this translates directly through
P
, since
P
is the identity on each of the laxitors.

7.
G
-gradings

For the remainder of the article, fix a finite group
G
and assume that
\mathcal{V}
is linear.

Definition 7.1
.

We say that a
\mathcal{V}
-category
\mathscr{C}
is
additive
if its underlying category is additive. We say a
\mathcal{V}
-functor between additive
\mathcal{V}
-categories is additive if its underlying functor is additive.

Definition 7.2
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
be
\mathcal{V}
-categories. We define the
external direct sum

\mathcal{A}\oplus\mathcal{B}
to be the
\mathcal{V}
-category with objects
a\oplus b
for
a\in\mathcal{A}
and
b\in\mathcal{B}
, and hom objects given by
\left(\mathcal{A}\oplus\mathcal{B}\right)\left(a_{1}\oplus b_{1}\to a_{2}\oplus b_{2}\right)\coloneqq\mathcal{A}\left(a_{1}\to a_{2}\right)\oplus\mathcal{B}\left(b_{1}\to b_{2}\right)
, using the direct sum on objects of
\mathcal{V}
.

Definition 7.3
.

A
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category
is a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category
\mathscr{C}
along with a decomposition
\mathscr{C}=\bigoplus_{g\in G}\mathscr{C}_{g}
, such that for each
c_{g}\in\mathscr{C}_{g}
and
c_{h}\in\mathscr{C}_{h}
, we have
c_{g}c_{h}\in\mathscr{C}_{gh}
. We say that the
G
-grading is
faithful
if for each
g\in G
there exist
a_{g},b_{g}\in\mathscr{C}_{g}
such that
\mathscr{C}_{g}(a_{g}\to b_{g})\neq 0_{\mathcal{V}}
. If
\mathscr{C}
and
\mathscr{D}
are
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories, a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functor
(\mathcal{F},\nu):\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}
is called
G
-graded if the underlying functor
F
is
G
-graded, i.e.,
F
is additive and for every
g\in G
and every
c_{g}\in C_{g}
we have
F(c_{g})\in\mathscr{D}_{g}
. We say that a
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functor
(\mathcal{F},\nu)
is an
equivalence
if it is a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal equivalence of
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories. Note that in this case,
\mathcal{F}|_{\mathscr{C}_{g}}:\mathscr{C}_{g}\to\mathscr{D}_{g}
is a
\mathcal{V}
-equivalence for all
g\in G
, and is a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal equivalence when
g=e
.

Definition 7.4
.

(
[
JMPP19
]
)
A
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor category consists of a linear monoidal category
C
, a decomposition
C=\bigoplus_{g\in G}C_{g}
into linear categories
C_{g}
, and a braided strong monoidal functor
\mathcal{F}_{C}:\mathcal{V}\to Z(C)
such that
\mathcal{F}_{C}^{Z}(\mathcal{V})\subseteq{\mathsf{Rep}}(G)^{\prime}\subseteq Z(C)
(equivalently,
\mathcal{F}_{C}(\mathcal{V})\subseteq C_{e}

[
JMPP19
, Lemma 2.11]
). Given
(C,\mathcal{F}_{C})
and
(D,\mathcal{F}_{D})

G
-graded tensored
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor categories, a morphism
(R,\rho,r):C\to D
is called
G
-graded if
R
is additive and for
g\in G
and
c_{g}\in C_{g}
,
R(c_{g})\in D_{g}
. We say that
(R,\rho,r)
is an
equivalence
if
(R,\rho)
is a strong monoidal equivalence and
r
is a natural isomorphism.

7.1.
G
-graded correspondence

On the way to a
G
-graded version of Theorem
1.2
, we define
G
-graded analogues to
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
and construct a correspondence on 0-cells.

Definition 7.5
.

Define the 2-category
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}
as follows:

•

0-cells are
G
-graded (weakly) tensored
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories

•

1-cells are
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functors

•

2-cells are
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal natural transformations.

The same proofs as in Section
3
show that
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}
is again a 2-category under the same compositions. Similarly, we define the 2-category
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}
via

•

0-cells are
G
-graded (weakly) tensored
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor categories

•

1-cells are
G
-graded monoidal functors with action-coherence natural transformations

•

2-cells are monoidal natural transformations satisfying the coherence in
3

Working towards extending Theorem
1.2
, we first extend Theorem
1.1
for the 0-cells:

Theorem 7.6
.

There is a bijective correspondence between equivalence classes:

\left\{\,\parbox{199.16928pt}{\rm Faithfully $G$-graded (weakly) tensored rigid $\mathcal{V}$-monoidal categories
$\mathscr{C}=\bigoplus_{g\in G}\mathscr{C}_{g}$
}\,\right\}\,\,\cong\,\,\left\{\,\parbox{213.39566pt}{\rm Faithfully $G$-graded
(weakly) tensored rigid $\mathcal{V}$-module tensor categories
$(C=\bigoplus_{g\in G}C_{g},\mathcal{F}_{C}^{\scriptscriptstyle Z})$
}\,\right\}.

Proof.

In the following, we revert to notation of
[
MP19
]
for clarity, with the underlying category of
\mathscr{C}
denoted by
\mathscr{C}^{\mathcal{V}}
, and the
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category associated to a
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor category
\left(C,\mathcal{F}_{C}\right)
being denoted by
C_{\mathbin{/\mkern-6.0mu/}\mathcal{F}}
. We use this to check that our abuse of notation is valid up to equivalence - here a
G
-graded monoidal equivalence. We will continue to use ordinary font in subscripts and superscripts to specify relation to the underlying category, e.g.,
C
refers to
\mathscr{C}^{\mathcal{V}}
. We first show that the correspondence in Theorem
1.1
can be extended to preserve
G
-gradings.

Suppose we start with a (weakly) tensored
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category
\mathscr{C}=\bigoplus_{g\in G}\mathscr{C}_{G}
. We show first that
\mathcal{F}_{C}\left(\mathcal{V}\right)\subseteq\mathscr{C}_{e}^{\mathcal{V}}
. Fix
b\in\mathscr{C}_{g}
for some nonidentity
g\in G
; we know
\mathscr{C}\left(1_{\mathscr{C}}\to b\right)\cong 0_{\mathcal{V}}
since
\mathscr{C}
is
G
-graded (and
1_{\mathscr{C}}\in\mathscr{C}_{e}
), so for all
v\in V
,

\displaystyle 0_{\mathrm{{\mathsf{Vec}}}}\cong\mathcal{V}\left(v\to\mathscr{C}\left(1_{\mathscr{C}}\to b\right)\right)\cong\mathscr{C}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(\mathcal{F}_{C}\left(v\right)\to b\right).

Thus
\mathscr{C}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(\mathcal{F}_{C}\left(v\right)\to b\right)\cong 0_{\mathrm{{\mathsf{Vec}}}}
for all
b
not in
\mathscr{C}^{\mathcal{V}}_{e}
, so
\mathcal{F}_{C}\left(\mathcal{V}\right)\subseteq\mathscr{C}_{e}
. We also have, with all direct sums over
g\in G
,

\displaystyle\mathscr{C}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(\bigoplus a_{g}\to\bigoplus b_{g}\right)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathscr{C}\left(\bigoplus a_{g}\to\bigoplus b_{g}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\bigoplus\mathscr{C}_{g}\left(a_{g}\to b_{g}\right)\right)

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathscr{C}_{g}\left(a_{g}\to b_{g}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\bigoplus\mathscr{C}_{g}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(a_{g}\to b_{g}\right),

so
\mathscr{C}^{\mathcal{V}}
is equivalent to
\oplus_{g}\mathscr{C}_{g}^{\mathcal{V}}
, and thus
(\mathscr{C}^{\mathcal{V}},\mathcal{F}_{C})
is a (weakly) tensored
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor category.

Now suppose we have a
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor category
(C=\bigoplus C_{g},\mathcal{F}_{C})
. Then we get a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category
C_{\mathbin{/\mkern-6.0mu/}\mathcal{F}}
by
5.1
. Further,
C\cong\bigoplus C_{g}
as
\mathcal{V}
-module categories with the actions
(v,c_{g})\mapsto c_{g}\mathcal{F}_{C}(v)
; this is valid because
\mathcal{F}_{C}\left(v\right)\subseteq C_{e}
, so
c_{g}\mathcal{F}_{C}\left(v\right)
is again in
C_{g}
. Since every element of
\mathscr{C}
can be written as a direct sum of objects from the
\mathscr{C}_{g}
, we have the following natural isomorphisms:

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}\left(v\to\mathscr{C}\left(\bigoplus a_{g}\to\bigoplus b_{g}\right)\right)

\displaystyle\cong\mathscr{C}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(\left(\bigoplus a_{g}\right)\mathcal{F}_{C}\left(v\right)\to\bigoplus b_{g}\right)

\displaystyle\cong\mathscr{C}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(\left(\bigoplus a_{g}\mathcal{F}_{C}\left(v\right)\right)\to\bigoplus b_{g}\right)

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus\mathscr{C}_{g}^{\mathcal{V}}\left(\left(a_{g}\mathcal{F}_{C}\left(v\right)\right)\to b_{g}\right)

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus\mathcal{V}\left(v\to\mathscr{C}_{g}\left(a_{g}\to b_{g}\right)\right)

\displaystyle\cong\mathcal{V}\left(v\to\bigoplus\mathscr{C}_{g}\left(a_{g}\to b_{g}\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{V}\left(v\to\left(\bigoplus\mathscr{C}_{g}\right)\left(\bigoplus a_{g}\to\bigoplus b_{g}\right)\right).

Now by the Yoneda Lemma we see that
\mathscr{C}
is equivalent to
\bigoplus\mathscr{C}_{g}
as
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories, so
\mathscr{C}
is a
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category.

To finish the proof, we see that in
[
MP19
, sections 6 and 7]
the authors construct a strong monoidal equivalence of categories
C\cong C_{\mathbin{/\mkern-6.0mu/}\mathcal{F}}^{\mathcal{V}}
, and extend it to an equivalence of
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor categories. They analogously construct an equivalence of the
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories
\mathscr{C}\cong\mathscr{C}_{\mathbin{/\mkern-6.0mu/}\mathcal{F}}^{\mathcal{V}}
. Both equivalences are the identity on objects, so both are
G
-graded.
∎

Theorem 7.7
.

Theorem
1.2
extends to an equivalence of 2-categories between
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}
.

Proof.

We construct a 2-functor
P_{G}:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}
in the same way as in Section
5
. The 0-cells in the image of
P_{G}
are
G
-graded by the above, and the 1-cells are
G
-graded since
P_{G}
doesn’t change how 1-cells act on objects; 2-cells are unchanged from the non-
G
-graded case. Since
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}
have the same composition as
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
, respectively, it follows that
P_{G}
is a 2-functor.

To check that
P_{G}
is a 2-equivalence, we again just need to check that it is essentially surjective on 0-cells, essentially surjective on 1-cells, and fully faithful on 2-cells. Essential surjectivity on 0-cells is exactly Theorem
7.6
.

Next, let
\mathscr{C}
and
\mathscr{D}
be 0-cells in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}
and consider a 1-cell
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho^{R}\right):\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}
in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
. Since
\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)=P\left(\mathcal{R}\right)\left(a\right)
for all objects
a\in\mathscr{C}
, it follows that
\mathcal{R}
is
G
-graded if and only if
P\left(\mathcal{R}\right)
is
G
-graded. Thus the same construction as for 1-cells in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
gives us a map from 1-cells in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}
to 1-cells in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}
. Since
P
is essentially surjective on 1-cells, it now follows that
P_{G}
is as well.

Given two 1-cells
\mathcal{R},\mathcal{S}
between
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal categories, note that
\mathcal{R}
and
\mathcal{S}
are still 1-cells in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
as well. Since 2-cells don’t have any inherent
G
-grading, we have
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}\left(\mathcal{R}\to\mathcal{S}\right)=\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}\left(\mathcal{R}\to\mathcal{S}\right)
. This also holds for
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}
, so
P_{G}
is fully faithful on 2-cells as before.
∎

8.
G
-extensions

Now fix a finite group
G
, a tensored
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category
\mathcal{A}
and its corresponding tensored
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor category
(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})
. For this section assume that
\mathcal{V}
is linear and
\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}
is strong monoidal.

In this section we extend Theorem
7.7
to the setting of
G
extensions of
\mathcal{A}
and
\left(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}\right)
. We construct
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
, prove a correspondence between zero cells, and extend the correspondence to an equivalence of 2-categories.

Definition 8.1
.

A
G
-graded extension
of
\mathcal{A}
is a faithfully
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category
\mathscr{C}=\bigoplus_{g\in G}\mathscr{C}_{g}
equipped with a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal equivalence
(\mathcal{I}^{C},\iota^{C}):\mathcal{A}\to\mathscr{C}_{e}
. For example, any faithfully
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal category
\mathscr{C}
, equipped with the identity on
\mathscr{C}_{e}
is a
G
-extension of
\mathscr{C}_{e}
. If
(\mathscr{C},\mathcal{I}^{C},\iota^{C})
and
(\mathscr{D},\mathcal{I}^{D},\iota^{D})
are
G
-extensions of
\mathcal{A}
. We define a morphism from
\mathscr{C}
to
\mathscr{D}
to be a triple
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho,p\right)
, where
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho\right)
is a
G
-graded strong
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal functor, and
p
is a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal natural transformation
p:\mathcal{I}^{D}\Rightarrow\mathcal{I}^{C}\circ\mathcal{R}_{e}
.

Definition 8.2
.

A
G
-graded extension
of
(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})

-graded rigid tensored
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor category

\mathcal{V}

\left(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}\right)

\left(R,\rho,r,p\right)

Definition 8.3
.

Define the 2-category
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}

G
-extensions of
\mathcal{A}
.

•

1-cells are the morphisms defined above.

•

2-cell are the
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded monoidal natural transformations
\theta:\left(\mathcal{R},\rho,p\right)\Rightarrow\left(\mathcal{S},\sigma,q\right):\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}
such that
\left(p_{a}\theta_{a}\right)\circ\left({-}\circ_{\mathscr{D}}{-}\right)=q_{a}
for each
a\in\mathscr{C}

We define the 2-category
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
via:

•

0-cells are the
G
-extensions of
\left(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z}\right)
.

•

1-cells are the morphisms defined above.

•

2-cells are the monoidal natural transformations
\Theta:\left(R,\rho,r,p\right)\Rightarrow\left(S,\sigma,s,q\right):C\to D
such that for all
v\in\mathcal{V}
,
r_{v}\circ\Theta_{\mathcal{F}_{C}\left(v\right)}=s_{v}
, and for all
a\in C
,
p_{a}\circ\Theta_{I^{C}\left(a\right)}=q_{a}
.

We again use the same compositions as for
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
, with the slight change that for 1-cells we now need to compose the new coherences
p
as well; we take the usual vertical composition of (
1_{\mathcal{V}}
-graded) monoidal natural transformations. All checks that
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
are 2-categories are analogous to the checks for
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
and
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}
.

Theorem 8.4
.

There is a bijective correspondence between equivalence classes

\left\{\,\parbox{113.81102pt}{$\mathcal{V}$-monoidal $G$-extensions \\
$(\mathscr{C}=\bigoplus_{g\in G}\mathscr{C}_{g},\mathcal{I},\iota)$ of $\mathcal{A}$
}\,\right\}\,\,\cong\,\,\left\{\,\parbox{170.71652pt}{\rm$G$-extensions \\
$(C=\bigoplus_{g\in G}C_{g},\mathcal{F}_{C}^{\scriptscriptstyle Z},I,i,\iota)$ of $(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}^{Z})$
}\,\right\}.

Proof.

From Theorem
7.6
, we have a correspondence of 0-cells
P_{G}:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}
. Given a 0-cell
\left(\mathscr{C},\mathcal{I},\iota\right)
in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
, we get a
G
-graded
\mathcal{V}
-module tensor category
\left(C,\mathcal{F}_{C}\right)
via the map on 0-cells induced by
P_{G}
. By the map on 1-cells induced by
P_{G}
, we also get a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal equivalence
\left(I,\iota,i\right)
from
\left(\mathcal{I},\iota\right)
. Thus we have a 0-cell
\left(C,\mathcal{F}_{C},I,\iota,i\right)
in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
. Further, since both of the induced maps from
P_{G}
are bijections on equivalence classes (of 0-cells and 1-cells, respectively), it follows that we get a bijection from equivalence classes of 0-cells in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
to 0-cells of
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
.
∎

8.1.
G
-extension 2-functor

We lift our 2-functor
P_{G}:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}
to a 2-functor
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
. On 0-cells, we begin the definition of
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
with the correspondence in Theorem
8.4
: From a 0-cell
(\mathscr{C},\mathcal{I}^{C},\iota^{C})
in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
, we use Theorem
8.4
to get a 0-cell in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
.

Given 0-cells
(\mathscr{C},\mathcal{I}^{C},\iota^{C})
,
(\mathscr{D},\mathcal{I}^{D},\iota^{D})
in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
and a 1-cell
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho,p\right)\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}\left(\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}\right)
, we construct the first three components of a 1-cell,
\left(R,\rho,r\right)
, as in Theorem
7.7
. Lastly, we need a coherence natural isomorphism
p
. We notice that

\displaystyle p_{a}\in\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathscr{D}\left(\mathcal{I}_{D}\left(a\right)\to\mathcal{S}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(\mathcal{I}_{B}\left(a\right)\right)\right)\right)\right)=D\left(I_{D}\left(a\right)\to S\left(R\left(I_{B}\left(a\right)\right)\right)\right),

so we use the same one, i.e., we take the mate of
p
under this identity adjunction.

which is the same as the mate of the left hand side above.
∎

Lastly, we need to work with 2-cells. Given 1-cells
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho,p\right),\left(\mathcal{S},\sigma,q\right):\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}
and a 2-cell
\theta:\mathcal{R}\Rightarrow\mathcal{S}
, we construct
\Theta:\left(R,\rho,r,p\right)\Rightarrow\left(S,\sigma,s,q\right)
via
\Theta_{a}=\theta_{a}
using the identity adjunction

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}\left(1_{\mathcal{V}}\to\mathscr{D}\left(\mathcal{R}\left(a\right)\to\mathcal{S}\left(a\right)\right)\right)=D\left(R\left(a\right)\to S\left(a\right)\right).

Lemma 8.6
.

Under these definitions, we have
p_{a}\circ\Theta_{I^{C}\left(a\right)}=q_{a}
.

Proof.

Taking mates on both sides gives exactly the coherence condition on
\theta
.
∎

Proposition 8.7
.

The above construction of
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
defines a 2-functor.

Proof.

We already have a map on 0-cells, and for each pair of 0-cells
\mathscr{C}
and
\mathscr{D}
in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}
, we can use the above maps on 1-cells and 2-cells to construct the functor

\displaystyle P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}{}_{\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}}:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}\left((\mathscr{C},\mathcal{I}^{C},\iota^{C})\to(\mathscr{D},\mathcal{I}^{D},\iota^{D})\right)\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{ModTens}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}\left(P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}\left((\mathscr{C},\mathcal{I}^{C},\iota^{C})\right)\to P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}\left((\mathscr{D},\mathcal{I}^{D},\iota^{D})\right)\right)

Now we just need to check that
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
as defined here is a 2-functor:

•

For each 0-cell
\left(\mathscr{C},\mathcal{I}^{C},\iota^{C}\right)
, both
\id_{P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}\left(\mathscr{C}\right)}
and
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}{}_{\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{C}}\left(\id_{\mathscr{C}}\right)
are the identity 1-cell on
\mathscr{C}
.

•

Composition of 1-cells is preserved by
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
. To see this, notice that the only change from Section
7.1
is that we now have an extra coherence natural transformation
p
. However,
p
is mapped directly to its mate under adjunction
4.1
, and mates preserve composition (Lemma
4.7
).

•

Composition of 2-cells is unchanged from previous sections, so both horizontal and vertical composition of 2-cells are preserved.

∎

8.2.
G
-extension equivalence

Now to finish the equivalence, we need to show that
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
is fully faithful and essentially surjective.

Lemma 8.8
.

The 2-functor
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
is essentially surjective on 0-cells.

Proof.

This is exactly Theorem
8.4
.
∎

Lemma 8.9
.

The 2-functor
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
is also essentially surjective on 1-cells.

Proof.

Given
\left(R,\rho,r,p\right):\left(C,I^{C},\iota^{C},i^{C}\right)\to\left(D,I^{D},\iota^{D},i^{D}\right)
a 1-cell of
G
-graded extensions of
\left(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}\right)
, we construct
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho\right)
as before, and again take mates under the identity adjunction for
p
. The only check needed to prove that
\left(\mathcal{R},\rho,p\right)
is a 1-cell in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
is to show that
p
is a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal natural transformation. Monoidality follows directly from taking mates and applying monoidality of
p

and this is exactly the mate of the left hand side. Thus we get a 1-cell in
\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\textbf{MonCat}_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
. With the exception of the new coherence natural transformation
p
, this map was already shown to be an essential inverse to
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
in Theorem
7.7
. But we’ve also inverted
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
for
p
, since
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
takes
p
to itself, so
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
is essentially surjective on 1-cells.
∎

Lemma 8.10
.

Lastly,
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
is fully faithful on 2-cells.

Proof.

Given
\left(R,\rho,r,p\right),\left(S,\sigma,s,q\right):\left(C,I^{C},\iota^{C},i^{C}\right)\to\left(D,I^{D},\iota^{D},i^{D}\right)
1-cells of
G
-extensions of
\left(A,\mathcal{F}_{A}\right)
and
\Theta:R\Rightarrow S
a 2-cell between them, we construct
\theta:\mathcal{R}\Rightarrow\mathcal{S}
via
\theta_{a}\coloneqq\Theta_{a}
, as before. We already know that
\theta
is a
\mathcal{V}
-monoidal natural transformation by the work before we introduced
G
-extensions. The last coherence on
\theta
follows immediately from taking mates as when we constructed
\Theta
going the other way in the previous section. Lastly, since we’re defining
\theta=\Theta
at the component level, this map is a bijection, and thus
P_{G}^{\mathcal{A}}
is fully faithful on 2-cells.
∎
